item.title: Introduction to Quarto
item.dc:creator: Darren Shoemaker
item.description:
Note

This is a reproduction of an introductory workshop on the Quarto ecosystem I gave during a lab meeting in the Krabbenhoft Aquatic Ecology lab.1

What is Quarto?

Quarto is a popular free and open-source (FOSS) technical publishing system used to create dynamic reports, dashboards, articles, presentations, books, and even websites.2 If you have worked in R for any length of time, you’ve almost certainly encountered Quarto content, even if you didn’t notice. Quarto is most commonly used alongside R, Python, and Julia, but supports an astonishing variety of coding languages and document formats. Quarto takes generic Markdown text as an input and renders a document in the desired format.

Because Quarto can do so many different things, the system can appear overwhelming. For those who learned programming languages such as R, Python, or Git, you likely remember particularly painful learning curves. Quarto is not like that! In fact, learning basic Quarto is refreshingly simple.

For this workshop, we’re mostly going to focus on using Quarto to produce reports, typically in the context of academic collaborations. Imagine you’re trying to share a statistical analysis in R with your advisor, graduate committee, or coauthors. Quarto can do a lot, but we want to keep things simple for now.

We will cover the three primary components of Quarto: the header, the markdown, and code chunks, and rendering your final document.

Getting Started

Checking Your Installation

First, we need to check if we have Quarto installed. Open the terminal and type or copy the following command:

quarto --version

If Quarto is installed, you should see a version number like 1.9.38. Quarto comes bundled with Positron and RStudio, so you likely already have it even if you haven’t used it.

If you don’t have Quarto installed, you can find the executable for your operating system from the Quarto website or install from the command line.

Windows

winget install Posit.Quarto

macOS

brew install --cask quarto

Creating a New Document

Staying organized is just as important for Quarto as any other file type. I recommend creating a new folder to keep all of your content in one place for this workshop. If you work in RStudio, you can create a new R Project with a .Rproj file to mark the working directory. If you are working in VSCode or Positron, you can just create a new folder.

Quarto files use the .qmd extension. To create your Quarto document, create a new file with a creative name, such as quarto_workshop.qmd. RStudio has an option in the new file dropdown to create a new Quarto document, which will pre-populate the document with some “helpful” defaults. If you are working in Positron, your file will be blank.

Anatomy of a Quarto Document

The YAML Header

Quarto documents are primarily defined by metadata included in a YAML header, which you might sometimes see referred to as frontmatter. This header includes important information about the document and sets rules for how different components will behave.

There are hundreds of possible combinations of these rules you could include, so for this workshop we’re only going to focus on what I think are the most immediately relevant. With that in mind, there are a few critical points I want you to remember:

  1. Every Quarto document must have a YAML header!
  2. Beyond the most basic formatting rules, these are mostly not worth committing to memory! Save your mental energy for ecological and statistical concepts that demand real understanding. You’ll learn what’s important out of habit.
  3. Spaces in a YAML header mean something! If a document is not rendering correctly, you almost certainly have an incorrect space somewhere.

Here is a basic example YAML header:

---
title: "Creative Title"
author: "Give Yourself the Credit You Deserve"
date: today
format: html
embed-resources: true
---

Your YAML header is marked by three hyphens (---). Each line inside describes a different rule for the document. In my opinion, title, author, date, and format are the most important. The title, author, and date appear at the top of the document after rendering.

You can type out a date if you want, for example, to pretend you didn’t make your document at the last minute, but you can also just use today to automatically populate the field with the date you saved the document.

The default output format for a Quarto document is html, so this field is also not strictly necessary. However, you may wish to change or add additional formats down the road, so I recommend getting used to including this.

I personally recommend always setting embed-resources: true as well. If you are using images, external fonts, a custom theme, or so on, this ensures they are stored with the document, which is useful for sharing. It’s annoying to share a document and realize all of the images are broken.

The YAML header for this document includes a few extra fields:

---
title: "Introduction to Quarto"
author: "Darren Shoemaker"
date: today
categories: 
format: 
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
    code-copy: true
embed-resources: true
---

First, notice the html argument appears below format:, instead of next to it. We do this because we are expanding the formatting rules with some additional fields. Also, note this is a place where spaces matter. Each additional field added beneath one must be exactly two spaces to the left, so html must be indented two spaces from format and toc and code-copy must be indented two spaces from html.

  • toc (table of contents) is another field I find myself using often. This automatically adds a table of contents to an HTML document, which can be really helpful for helping collaborators navigate your report.
  • toc-depth defines the level of headers that are included in the table of contents. You can tweak this depending on how long your document ends up and how many subheadings you end up using.
  • code-copy adds a copy button to code chunks, just like the ones on this page. This can be useful if you want others to be able to follow along with an analysis, saving them typing and likely preventing errors.

The Text Body

I think the most compelling reason to use Quarto is the ability to seamlessly integrate plain text, code, and analysis outputs including graphs and tables. This makes it easy to share your work with collaborators, even those who may not know R!

In practice, I find this commonly looks like a header defining a major section of an analysis, such as “Data Cleaning,” “Summary Statistics,” or “Visualizations,” followed by the relevant code chunk, and finally a plain text interpretation explaining what you think the output means.

Any text written directly in a Quarto document is interpreted as plain text. Use #s to add headers, which will also show up in the table of contents.

Header Level Syntax Example
Level 1 # # Heading Level 1 (Largest)
Level 2 ## ## Heading Level 2
Level 3 ### ### Heading Level 3
Level 4 #### #### Heading Level 4
Level 5 ##### ##### Heading Level 5
Level 6 ###### ###### Heading Level 6 (Smallest)

Code Chunks

Code chunks are the “dynamic” component of a Quarto document. To add a code chunk, type three backticks (```), followed by brackets {}, and add three more backticks on a new line. Everything in between the two sets of backticks is interpreted as code. You can define the coding language you’re using by typing it inside the brackets, such as {r}. In RStudio and Positron, use the keyboard shortcut ctrl+alt+i to automatically insert an R code chunk.

For example, we’re going to use the classic “iris” dataset from Ronald Fisher. We will load the data, inspect the dataframe with head(), plot flower petal lengths and widths by species, and finally add a legend.

# Load the iris dataset
data(iris)

# Display the first few rows of the dataset
head(iris)
  Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species
1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2  setosa
2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2  setosa
3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2  setosa
4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2  setosa
5          5.0         3.6          1.4         0.2  setosa
6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4  setosa
# Create a scatter plot of petal length vs width, colored by species
plot(Petal.Length ~ Petal.Width, col = Species, data = iris, pch = 19)

# Add a legend to identify the species
legend(
  x = "topleft",
  legend = levels(iris$Species),
  col = 1:3,
  pch = 19,
  title = "Species"
)

Looks like virginica has the largest flowers. Who would have guessed?

Here is where I think the real strength of Quarto shines through. Imagine instead of the iris dataset, you instead needed to share the outcome of an analysis with your dissertation committee. You now your actual code, your figures and plots, and your interpretation. This means you can show your code to the collaborators who want to see it, and your interpretations to those who may not care about the nuance, all in one document!

Code Chunk Options

Just like the YAML header at the top of the document, you can also set options for individual code chunks. These have to appear at the top of the code chunk, and are marked with a # followed by a vertical bar |. These are useful if you want to modify the output of one code chunk without applying the options to every code chunk.

Warnings

The following code intentionally produces a warning because we’re taking the log of values that include non-positive numbers:

# This plot intentionally produces a warning due to log transformation of non-positive values
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Petal.Width - 0.2, log = "y", col = 'green', pch = 19)

In this case, the warning is important. R will drop non-positive values prior to the log transformation, which means we end up losing data points on the plot. However, what if the warning is not important? We can hide warnings by adding #| warning: false to the top of the code chunk.

Eval

One of the drawbacks to Quarto is each code chunk has to be evaluated, or run, each time the document is rendered. This takes less than a second for this document, which is just base R plots and some text, but can be slow with real statistical analyses. Another useful option is #| eval: false, which keeps the code chunk in the document, but does not actually run it.

# This code chunk will appear in the document but will not be executed
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Petal.Width - 0.2, log = "y", col = 'green', pch = 19)

Here, the code still appears, but because R did not actually run the line, neither the plot nor the warning are included.

Echo

If you want to hide the code completely, you can use #| echo: false. “echo” means “repeat” or “include,” so marking this option as false just means not including the code in the document.

Warning in xy.coords(x, y, xlabel, ylabel, log): 34 y values <= 0 omitted from
logarithmic plot

Note the code chunk doesn’t appear, but the warning and plot still show up. What gives? We set #| echo: false, but we did not set #| eval: false, so the code still executed and produced an output.

Output

If we want to show and run the code, but hide the output, we can use #| output: false. I don’t use this one often, but if the output of a code chunk is especially messy, this can be helpful.

# The code will run and produce a plot, but the text output will be hidden
plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Petal.Width - 0.2, log = "y", col = 'green', pch = 19)

Include

Finally, you can set #| include: false if you have code that you want to run, but hide both the output and code chunks. Typically this is used to hide libraries and other setup information, but for most of my use cases I want to make it clear what libraries I use, so I don’t use this often either.

As with the YAML headers, there are many other options for code chunks. These are just a small sample of ones you’ll use frequently.

Rendering Your Report

Once you have all the content you want to include, it’s time to render the document. If you set format: html or did not specify the format, rendering the document will produce a .html file with the same name as your report.

Both RStudio and Positron have a checkbox on the upper left of the script window that says “render on save.” This is fine for our simple example, but there are a few points of caution. If you save often, this will re-render the document every time you save. Because saving frequently is best practice (your dog might unplug your computer), this can bog down your computer for highly complex documents that take a long time to render.

Personally, I recommend rendering from the terminal instead. When you are ready to finalize your document, enter the following command into the terminal:

quarto render

This will render the document in the desired format, but you won’t have to re-render more times than necessary.

Using the terminal is also best practice if you want to render multiple formats at once. Positron has a quirk where using the render button directly in the IDE will only render one of the formats. For example, if I decided I wanted both an HTML and a PDF document, such as:

---
title: "Introduction to Quarto"
author: "Darren Shoemaker"
format: 
  html:
  pdf:
---

Only the HTML document would be created. This behavior is inconsistent and annoying, but rendering from the terminal always works, so I think this is just best practice.

Once you have the document, you’re done! Share your document just as you would any other. You may not be used to .html files, but these open in any web browser.

Beyond the Basics

That’s all we’re going to cover today, but Quarto is highly extensible, so if there’s more you want to explore, I recommend digging into the official documentation or just a simple web search.

References

  1. Krabbenhoft, C. Krabbenhoft Aquatic Ecology Lab. https://coreykrabbenhoft.com/. Accessed November 20, 2026.
  2. Posit, Inc. Quarto Documentation. https://quarto.org/docs/. Accessed November 20, 2026.

item.title: How to Start a Journal Article
item.dc:creator: Darren Shoemaker
item.description:
The First Sentence is the Hardest

One of the most important yet critically under-explained transitions in academia is the shift from writing research papers as a student to writing manuscripts for publication in a scholarly journal. Ideally, this transition will occur gradually during a master’s or PhD program with input and training from your advisor and committee. In practice, however, the last few months of a graduate program are often an overwhelming spring to complete a thesis or dissertation in time for a defense, and publishing is pushed to the side. Suddenly, the former student has graduated and is considered an early-career professional, where they are expected to already be familiar with academic writing.

My goal is to demystify the process of starting a journal article. You may be at the beginning of a new study, or you may have already completed an experiment and decided its worthy of its own publication. Check out this xkcd comic to see where your project fits. Every project and structure is different, so I can’t promise every step will be relevant. I am also still learning and growing every day, so what works for me may not work for everyone. Think critically about how you prefer to work and adapt these guidelines as you see fit.

The most important part is to actually start writing.

Start with Your Research Question

What question are you trying to answer?

Having a specific research question allows your paper to follow a clear narrative structure:

A strong research question is specific and explicit, minimizing ambiguity both to yourself and your colleagues about what you want to accomplish. An example research question from one of my recent papers:

“Our research objective was to identify the relationship between fish community structure and climatic variables in channelised agricultural headwater streams in northeast Indiana and central Ohio.”1

You also want to be sure to contextualize your research question in the broader scientific literature. Has your question been asked before in a different setting? Are you trying to reproduce or re-examine an existing study or is your question novel? How does your research question support or critique existing understanding?

Developing your research question early helps to maintain focus as you write. This can make the process seem less overwhelming by reducing spurious tangents or stream-of-consciousness that don’t actually help to answer your research question. Get in the habit of asking yourself how each sentence contributes to your overall objective. If you don’t have a good answer, what you’re writing may not serve your overall goals.

Beware of Hidden Objectives

You may end up revising your research question a few times during your writing process, both for clarity and as you gain a better understanding of possible hidden objectives, which are particularly common in applied research.

A hidden objective often emerges during writing, particularly in sentences such as “We examined [study organism] to better understand [study system] to inform [management/policy/regulatory group].” Often, the first draft of a research objective may omit or overlook the last part of the statement. Who or what will benefit from your study? If you are attempting to provide information to a group, should that be included in your research question? Is your overall goal just to gain understanding, or to provide information? Nothing is wrong with either approach, but be thoughtful about your goals and the implications of your results when developing your research question.

Outline your Process

What needs to happen to answer your research question?

Once you have explicitly defined your research question, start thinking about your research process. What type of information do you need to answer that question? How will that information be obtained? What analyses or visualizations will you need to turn that information into usable data? How will you present your results?

These questions are challenging and important, but you don’t need to know exactly how to answer them right now. Just have a vague sense of what you will need to do. Personally, I like using bulleted lists to outline this part, but find a structure that makes sense for you. Just write out step-by-step, breaking down as much as possible, what you think needs to happen to answer your research question.

“Step 1: Acquire Data”

This is not useful. You don’t provide any information to you or your collaborators and may give a sense you don’t really understand the work that needs to be done. Instead, try writing something like:

“Step 1: obtain landcover data for Erie County, NY, from USGS National Landcover database through the Google Earth Engine API.”

This version is specific, can easily be tied back to your research question, and most importantly, is an actionable step you can look back to if you get stuck later.

Your outline should be a living document as you will almost certainly end up revising it. Some steps may prove unfeasible, you might find more specific sub-steps are helpful, or you may end up removing a section from a publication. All of these are completely normal, as long as your revisions relate back to your research question.

Identify your Target Journal(s)

Depending on the stage of your research, this might not be realistic, but in generally I recommend identifying a few potential target journals as early as possible. Consider where the papers you cite are often published, the impact factor, any article processing charges, and the reputation of the journal. The nuances of journal selection warrant their own post, but having journals in mind is helpful for the next step.

Find your Collaborators

Finally, now that you’re armed with a solid research question, an outline of your methods, and have a few journals in mind, think of who you want to bring on to the project. You likely know a few people with expertise relevant to your idea, but remember the more people are involved, the more feedback you’ll have to consider before you can submit.

Being transparent with your potential collaborators is critically important. Be honest about how much information you have, how long you think your analysis will take, and your own limitations. If you have a step in your process that you have no idea how to accomplish, be up front about that. Not knowing a certain method or technique is not bad - that may be why you’re reaching out for help in the first place - but misrepresenting your own expertise is problematic. Remember that this likely won’t be the only time you work with these individuals, so making a good first impression matters.

Similarly, be up front about what you can offer collaborators. Do you intend to make them all authors on the paper? How much do you expect them to contribute to earn authorship? What is your anticipated author order? These conversations can be uncomfortable, but they are crucial to strong collaborations.

In general, the more information you can provide to your potential collaborators, the more informed decisions and support they can offer. Don’t take it personally if they are not interested in contributing to your project - they have a better understanding of their own limitations than you do.

Wrapping Up

At this point, you should have a solid foundation to start writing. Your research question guides your overall objective. The context of your research can be used to add background information in the introduction and the outline of your research process can be used as a map for your methods section.

Once you have results, just write them out exactly as they appear. You can always revise later, but I recommend getting them on paper as quickly as possible. This helps keep collaborators informed of your progress and prevents you from forgetting or losing potentially important information.

Beyond the first sentence, the discussion section is likely the most challenging, because every discussion is unique to a research project. In general, you want to contextualize your results. As your introduction described gaps in current understanding, your discussion examines how well your study filled those gaps, and identifies those that remain. You should also use this section to address any limitations of your methods, and how you (or others) might address them in the future. Finally, you can describe any broader implications of your research and how your findings might impact the world around you.

Starting a manuscript seems overwhelming, but by breaking down the process into manageable steps, you can move a lot faster than you might think. Remember that the most important thing is to just start writing.

References

  1. Shoemaker, D. J., P. C. Smiley, and R. B. Gillespie. 2025. “ Evaluating the Influence of Climatic and Hydrologic Variables on Fish Communities in Channelised Agricultural Headwater Streams in the Midwestern USA.” Freshwater Biology 70, no. 12: e70148. https://doi.org/10.1111/fwb.70148.

item.title: Coding for Sharing and Collaboration
item.dc:creator: Darren Shoemaker
item.description:
NoteNote

This content was originally published as a part of the MSU WFA Coding Club and my tools and process have evolved somewhat since then. However, I stand by the philosophy of this post, and the strategies described here are still a good starting point for beginners looking to be more thoughtful about their data science projects.

Introduction

Today we’re going to discuss how to share code with your committee or collaborators. An unfortunately frequent event during graduate school is to spend weeks or months developing a script, share that script with your committee member, and the script fails when they try to run it. What happened? It worked perfectly yesterday! As always, my solution is not the only solution, so if you find something which works better, absolutely do that (and maybe tell me so I don’t keep doing stuff the hard way). The idea is that your collaborator(s) should be able to simply click run on a .R script and obtain the same output as you.

A useful heuristic I like is to ask myself, “Would my friend be able to run my script on their laptop at our Arctic research base?” If the answer is yes*, you’re already done, but if you’re not sure, keep reading!

*If you are working with extremely large files or computationally intensive tasks, their laptop may not be able to run the script anyway, so assume a relatively normal analysis.

[1] Working in Projects

The easiest way to collaborate is to work inside of an intuitively named R Project using a .Rproj file. I wrote a simple guide on using R Projects which you can read here. Remember that a project is a self-contained directory which should contain all the components needed to run an analysis. In general, I keep data, output, scripts, and temp folders inside project directories, but adapt this to your own needs.

Projects are helpful for collaboration because the entire project can be shared as a .zip file. I personally use the program 7-zip to create zip files, but Windows has a native function. Right click on the project directory and click Add to [PROJECT_NAME.zip]. I am going to use R_organized_house from the staying organized guide as an example.

You should end up with a .zip archive with the same name as your project directory.

This is the folder you will share with your collaborators. Remember they will need to unzip the folder before they can start working with your project.

[2] Packages and Libraries

The .R script file you actually them to run should be inside the zipped archive. Once they unzip the folder, they can open the .Rproj file in their own local RStudio environment.

This guide requires the here() library. As with all libraries, they have to be loaded before we can use the functions in them. You have almost certainly used the line library([PACKAGE_NAME|) in a script before.

Libraries

Begin every script with a code chunk which loads the necessary libraries. This will ensure whoever runs the script after you will be able to access the functions you use.

# Libraries

library(here)

Depending on if you’ve used here() before, you may see the following error.

For the sake of argument, we’ll assume our friend in the Arctic has not used the here() library and does receive the error. This means the script has already failed before we have begun any analysis or even loaded our data.

This means the user has not installed the package. This brings us to a crossroads so I’m going to get on a soapbox: As a general rule, I do not want my scripts to modify the end users’ computer. This means I do not want to install new software or write new files. If your collaborator trusts you, and I hope they do, they probably won’t care, but I think this is best practice from a coding, data management, and privacy perspective. However, without installing the package, the script won’t work.

My workaround is to provide the installation code but commented out. The user can use their own due diligence and review if they want to install the package, and that the install.packages() function will be skipped over if they already have the package and installation is unnecessary. This will look something like the following code chunk.

# Install Packages

#install.packages('here')
#install.packages('ggplot2')

# Libraries 

library(here)
library(ggplot2)

[3] Reading in Data

Once our friend has loaded the appropriate libraries, they need to access any data read in by the script. A common trap is to use the function setwd() to access files.

This works fine on my computer. The issue is E: is my external hard drive, R_Stuff keeps backups of my work, and coding_club is a local directory I use for the website. My friend has none of these folders! This means any script which uses this line will only work exactly on my computer and if I don’t change anything about my folders. Unlikely!

The here() package is my preferred method for accessing a working directory in a collaborative setting. This package works by automatically (magically) setting the working directory to the highest folder associated with the R Project. This works by looking for .Rproj, .gitignore, or another high-level file which applies to the entire project. This should occur as soon as the library is loaded, but you can double check by calling the here::here() function.

here::here()

This function will identify where the term “here” is referring to. In my case, this is the coding_club folder I used to build this website.

For the purposes of this example, I am going to read in the filtered virginca_processed .csv which we made in the Staying Organized guide. Another good practice is to use head(), str(), or your preferred summary function to make sure the dataframe you read in looks like what you expect.

dat <- read.csv(file = here('posts/codingcollaboration/data', 'virginica_processed.csv'))
head(dat)

This looks like the iris dataset filtered to only include the species virginica. This is what I expected, so we’re ready to move on.

[4] Using the Data

If we have done everything described above correctly, our friend in the Arctic should now have the filtered iris dataframe, named dat, in their R environment. Sharing the data and files associated with an R script or project is probably 90% of the battle, so take a deep breath.

As an example, we’re going to make a couple plots using these data in the ggplot package, but substitute any analysis you want to share.

plot_1 <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = dat, mapping = aes(x = Petal.Width, y = Petal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_point(color = 'blue') +
  xlab('Petal Width') +
  ylab('Petal Length') +
  ggtitle('Length and Width of Virginica Petals in Sample')

plot_1

plot_2 <- ggplot2::ggplot(data = dat, mapping = aes(x = Sepal.Width, y = Sepal.Length, fill = Species)) +
  geom_point(color = 'blue') +
  xlab('Sepal Width') +
  ylab('Sepal Length') +
  ggtitle('Length and Width of Virginica Sepals in Sample')


plot_2

[5] Saving Outputs

Similarly to installing packages, I don’t like writing new files to another user’s computer. Still, many researchers will want to be able to access output files after running a script. I always try to provide the code to get the output, but again commented out. You may just want to reach out to your collaborators to clarify their preferences if the commented codes are annoying.

#ggsave(plot_1, file = here('output', 'plot_1.png'), dpi = 300)
#ggsave(plot_2, file = here('output', 'plot_2.png'), dpi = 300)

Again, the here() function lets us write the files to the output folder contained in the project directory. This means the images are written to the same place no matter who runs the script.

[6] General Best Practices for Shared Scripts

Congratulations! If you’ve made it this far, you should be able to write a script anyone can run. This section just adds a few extra tips which may be helpful. I will update this section relatively frequently so feel free to share anything you want added.

1. Comment Thoroughly

Just because your friend is able to run the script, it may not be immediately clear what each section of the script is doing. I recommend adding comments to the code to guide them through what each major section does. This will also be helpful to you in the future if you have to revisit an old project.

# Read data

## Generate plots

# Mixed effects modeling for fish abundance ----

#' The output from this model suggests water temperature has a positive effect on fish abundance.

There are a few strategies to commenting. You don’t need to write a research paper in the script, but some guidance can clarify complex code. Different types of comments only marginally change the script, but can affect the output if you knit the script into a different document.

The number of # symbols indicate the level of header. Incidentally, the Introduction header of this page uses #, each section uses ##, and the subsections in [6] use ###.

Adding the four minus signs after a comment will turn that into a section which can be accessed from the outline button in the top right of the script window. This is useful if your script is very long.

The apostrophe after the last comment indicates that this is a roxygen comment. This won’t change anything here, but indicates the comment should be treated as plain text in an HTML or PDF document.

2. Call Functions Explicitly

You may have noticed the double colon operators before some of the functions above.

::

This operator is used before calling a function to explicitly define the package namespace of that function. In our case, we used the following.

ggplot2::ggplot()
here::here()

This operator indicates to R that we want to use the ggplot() function from the ggplot2 package. In some cases, multiple functions from different packages may have the same name. This means that one will mask the other. R will provide a warning when you load libraries which share package names, but this is easy to miss.

We probably don’t know every package our friend has installed on their machine. By using the :: operator, we can make sure every function is running from the correct package. This may also save some headache if you accidentally mask a function down the road.

[7] Sharing the Project

With that, you should be prepared to share your analysis with your committee or collaborators! Hopefully they respond in a timely manner. Once you have everything in a .zip archive, you can share through email, a thumb drive, OneDrive/cloud service, or maybe even GitHub. As always, thank you for reading and please reach out with any feedback!

item.title: Staying Organized with R Projects
item.dc:creator: Darren Shoemaker
item.description:
NoteNote

This content was originally published as a part of the MSU WFA Coding Club and my tools and process have evolved somewhat since then. However, I stand by the philosophy of this post, and the strategies described here are still a good starting point for beginners looking to be more thoughtful about their data science projects.

Introduction

One of (in my opinion) the most useful and least-taught skills one can develop is how to stay organized in R. Here, I am going to present my technique for keeping my projects organized. As you read this, keep a few points in mind. This is neither the only nor the best strategy, so if this does not work for you, try something else. The most important thing is an organization system works for you and that you apply it consistently. If you start making exceptions or deviate from your system, you may not be able to find something later.

Two notes:

1) This guide will assume some familiarity with .R and .csv files and Windows folder system. If you are using a MacOS, this should translate pretty easily. If you are using a Linux Machine, you probably don’t need this guide.

2) All of my other coding_club pages will follow this organizational structure, so I recommend reading this one first.

Why is this so important?

Short answer: It may not be. Decide for yourself if devoting time up front will be worth the time you save down the road.

Long answer: As you use R more for classes, theses, and projects, you will find yourself making dozens to hundreds of scripts with all the associated data, outputs, and objects associated with each. If you, or better yet, your R environment, knows where to find everything it needs to function, you will save yourself time and headaches when you need to access these again. In academia and science, it is fairly common to step away from a project for months or even years at a time. The more detailed your organizational system, the easier it will be to pick these projects back up.

Step 1: Everything Needs a Home

Start by making a folder for all of your R stuff. Everything we do from this point on will happen inside this folder. R is a programming language which means it is very particular about how commands are entered. One aspect of this is that R does not like spaces. Always place an underscore _ or other character between terms. I will literally name this file R_Stuff. You can’t get more descriptive than that. If you like clumsy allegories, call R_Stuff our house.

Step 2: Maintaining a Consistent Folder Structure

Start by making a folder inside of R_Stuff. This can be anything, but remember the name can’t have any spaces. The name should also be descriptive. Someone who is not familiar with the folder or its contents (read: you in a couple months) should reasonably be able to guess what the folder contains. Consider this a room inside the house.

So, anyone who clicks on this folder will expect to see files related to a project called organized house.

Inside R_organized_house, we’re going to make a few more folders. These can also be named anything. You want them to be descriptive enough to make their contents clear, but general enough to reuse for multiple projects. I like, at minimum, including data, output, scripts, and temp folders. Think of these as desks or closets in the room.

Inside data, we’re going to go one step further and add a raw and processed folder. The raw data folder is the junk drawer. We can toss whatever into here without really thinking. The processed folder is tool drawer, which is hopefully more organized. We’ll write cleaned data to this folder.

Step 3: The R Project File

Finally, are ready to move into R. Begin by opening RStudio. If you feel the need, you can cry a bit. This is a healthy emotional release and R is scary. Once you’re ready, move to the file tab and click New Project.

The R Project is one of the most powerful tools for organization, but rarely mentioned in statistics courses. This is not the fault of the instructors - those courses are already packed with more material than can be reasonably taught. An RStudio project is associated with your working directory and creates a shortcut to open everything in that directory in your RStudio session.

In the next menu, click Existing Directory. New Directory is also fine, but we already set up our file structure. Version Control is the scary basement. Stay out of the basement.

Navigate to the folder you made previously. In our case, this is R_organized_house. Best practice is check open in new session. This is not completely necessary, but you probably don’t want anything from your current environment being used in the new project.

After you click create project, you’ll see a .Rproj file in the directory you picked.

The .Rproj file is the foundation of the organization system we’re using here. Whenever you want to work on your project, open Rstudio by clicking on the .Rproj file. In this case, R_organized_house. This will ensure you are working within that project directory, and any files or output you generate will stay in this folder.

Step 4: Working with Scripts and Data

Once you have a project set up, you’re finally to begin working! A .R script is is probably the most fundamental file type to the R programming language. Any scripts you make will have a .R file extension. To take full advantage of the folder structure we made, we’re going to use the here library. This is a powerful library for collaboration and we will only be scratching the surface of its functionality. Install the package if needed, then load the library.

The here package automatically sets the working directory to the highest folder in the project. The package begins working as soon as you load the library, but you can also call the here::here() function if you want to set the working directory manually. The function works by looking for a .Rproj file, .gitignore file, and a few others. Conveniently, we have a .Rproj file at the main folder, so the working directory above is set to coding_club. As you are probably working with a different folder name, double that this is set correctly.

The here library

library(here)

Because we set the working directory using here(), we have to use the here() function when reading or writing data. This may seem like an extra step, but I promise will save time in the long run. We will use the famous Iris dataset for this example. Iris is pre-loaded into R, but we will read it as a .csv file from the raw data folder.

data <- read.csv(file = here('data/raw', 'iris.csv'))

This is a bit more complicated than the usual read.csv(), so let’s break it down. We’re creating a data object as normal, but we have to tell R where to look for the file since we didn’t use set.wd(). To do this, we add the here() function to the file argument, and tell R that the file is inside the ‘data/raw’ folder. Because the data is in a folder inside a folder, we have to add the / between data and raw to indicate the file path. Finally, we name the file to tell R which file we want assigned to the object ‘data’.

head(data)

We’re going to make a simple change to the iris dataset for the purposes of this example. First, load the dplyr library and make a modification.

library(dplyr)

data <- data %>% 
  filter(Species == 'virginica')

head(data)

A Note on Filtering

The filter() function may be new so we’ll walk through that. We start with the data object we made earlier, then we’re going to use the pipe operator, &>&. The pipe operator is just a way to tell R to do something and then do something else. Here, we’re telling R to take the data object “and then” apply the filter function. The filter function tells R to take all the Species which are exactly equal ( == ) to virginica, so we make a new data object which only includes virginica.

Step 5: Using the Output and Temp Folders

Let’s go back to the house analogy. We’re still in the same room, the R_organized_house folder, but we want to put the data object somewhere else, maybe taking it out of the junk drawer and putting it somewhere more sensible. To do this, we’re going to use the here() function along with the folder structure we made at the beginning.

write.csv(data, file = here('output', 'virginica_output.csv'), row.names = F)

write.csv(data, file = here('temp', 'virginica_temp.csv'), row.names = F)

write.csv(data, file = here('data/processed', 'virginica_processed.csv'), row.names = F)

We actually wrote the same file to three different locations. In practice, you probably wouldn’t do this, but we can demonstrate the flexibility of the this approach. Because we’re using the here() function, we don’t need to set the working directory or write the entire file path. We just say that we’re here(). Conveniently, this is the top level folder, so what we’re really telling R is to make a .csv file here, inside either the output, temp, or data/processed folder. Typically, you would write results or tables to the output folder, something more experimental or exploratory to the temp folder, and a finalized, clean to dataset to the processed folder. This approach is also flexible, so you can add folders as needed. Maybe you want a folder for rasters inside of the data folder, or you want to sort your outputs more. Adapt as needed.

The Next Steps: the Project Template

So you’ve made one project, but your next class assignment is coming up and you want to make another folder. To keep the analogy, move to a different room, but that was a lot of effort. We’re going to make a project template to save a few steps. Make a new folder inside of R_Stuff. Mine is named project_template, but pick a name that works for you. I also lead with the digits 01, so the folder is always at the top of the R_Stuff directory.

Inside of this folder, make data, output, scripts, and temp folders, or whatever you folders you want in all or most of your projects. These should generally be empty, but if you have many projects which share a dataset, you may want to add these to the data/raw folder. From here, any time you want to make a new project, you can just copy the entire template folder, change the name to your new project, and then make a project with the new folder as the directory. I go one step further and also keep a read_data script in the scripts folder of the template, which saves me typing a few lines.

#' ---
#' title: "Read Data"
#' author: "Darren Shoemaker"
#' ---

# Libraries 

library(here)
library(tidyverse)

#read in data ----

dat <- read.csv(file = here('data/raw', ''))

Congratulations!

This is a basic rundown of how I keep my R projects organized. I hope this was helpful! If something is missing or unclear, please let me know. I want to make these as practical and useful as possible, so I appreciate your feedback. Now go do some great science!
